marrow__ANAT_CH59_Q001.takeaway: A foramen transversarium in each transverse process is characteristic of cervical vertebrae.
marrow__ANAT_CH59_Q001.displayText:
A foramen transversarium in each transverse process is characteristic of cervical vertebrae.

Typical cervical vertebrae are characterized by a foramen in the transverse process called the foramen transversarium. This transmits the vertebral artery and vein along with a branch from the cervicothoracic ganglion (vertebral nerve). Lateral parts of the transverse processes also contain anterior and posterior tubercles.

The source compares typical cervical and thoracic vertebrae in the retained table.
emphasis: A foramen transversarium in each transverse process is characteristic of cervical vertebrae

rationales.a: Cervical spinous processes are usually shorter and often bifid; long overlapping spines are typical of thoracic vertebrae.
rationales.c: Thoracic vertebral bodies are larger than their vertebral foramina; the reversed proportion is not a distinguishing feature.
rationales.d: Costal facets, rather than tubercles, mark thoracic transverse processes for rib articulation.

marrow__ANAT_CH59_Q002.takeaway: The conventional total is 33 vertebrae: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral and usually 4 coccygeal.
marrow__ANAT_CH59_Q002.displayText:
The conventional total is 33 vertebrae: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral and usually 4 coccygeal.

The vertebral column consists of 33 bones. The source lists 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 4 coccygeal vertebrae, while noting frequent variability and reported totals between 32 and 35.

The vertebral column is about 70 cm long in males and about 60 cm in females on average and functions in support, protection of the spinal cord and nerves, muscle attachment and hematopoiesis.
emphasis: The conventional total is 33 vertebrae: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral and usually 4 coccygeal

rationales.a: Twenty-seven omits many vertebrae, including most of the thoracic and lumbar regions.
rationales.b: Twenty-nine is below the standard sum of 33 vertebral elements.
rationales.c: Thirty-one does not equal the conventional regional total; coccygeal number varies but is usually four.

marrow__ANAT_CH59_Q003.takeaway: The cervical curve is normally lordotic; kyphosis is the normal thoracic and pelvic curvature.
marrow__ANAT_CH59_Q003.displayText:
The cervical curve is normally lordotic; kyphosis is the normal thoracic and pelvic curvature.

The cervical-kyphosis pair is incorrectly matched. The cervical part normally demonstrates lordosis.

During embryonic life the body is flexed and has primary thoracic and pelvic curves, which are convex dorsally. After birth, functional muscle development produces secondary cervical and lumbar curves, which are concave forwards (lordosis).

Normal adult curvatures: cervical lordosis, thoracic kyphosis, lumbar lordosis, pelvic curve concave anteroinferiorly.
emphasis: The cervical curve is normally lordotic; kyphosis is the normal thoracic and pelvic curvature

rationales.b: Thoracic kyphosis is a normal primary curvature, so this pair is correctly matched.
rationales.c: Lumbar lordosis is the normal secondary curvature, so this pair is correctly matched.
rationales.d: The pelvic curve is a normal primary kyphotic curve, concave anteriorly, which is consistent with the stated direction.

marrow__ANAT_CH59_Q004.takeaway: The thoracic curve is a primary curvature present during fetal life; it does not first appear when an infant walks.
marrow__ANAT_CH59_Q004.displayText:
The thoracic curve is a primary curvature present during fetal life; it does not first appear when an infant walks.

The thoracic curvature is a primary curve and develops during embryonic life itself; therefore the statement that it develops when the infant starts walking is false.

Primary thoracic and pelvic curves are convex dorsally. Secondary cervical curvature develops with muscles responsible for head extension; secondary lumbar curvature develops with muscles responsible for sitting upright and walking.
emphasis: The thoracic curve is a primary curvature present during fetal life; it does not first appear when an infant walks

rationales.a: Primary thoracic and pelvic curves are convex posteriorly, so this statement is accurate.
rationales.c: Cervical lordosis develops as the infant raises and supports the head.
rationales.d: Lumbar lordosis develops with upright posture and walking, making this statement accurate.

marrow__ANAT_CH59_Q005.takeaway: The craniocervical junction involves the occipital bone, atlas and axis; the sphenoid wings are not part of these joints.
marrow__ANAT_CH59_Q005.displayText:
The craniocervical junction involves the occipital bone, atlas and axis; the sphenoid wings are not part of these joints.

The craniocervical joints do not include the wings of the sphenoid. They connect the cranium to the vertebral column and include the atlanto-occipital and atlanto-axial joints; the bones involved include occipital condyles, atlas and axis.

The source notes occipitocervical fusion/stabilization as treatment for conditions including trauma, rheumatoid arthritis, congenital malformations, neoplasms and degeneration.
emphasis: The craniocervical junction involves the occipital bone, atlas and axis; the sphenoid wings are not part of these joints

rationales.a: The atlas forms the atlanto-occipital and atlanto-axial articulations of the junction.
rationales.b: The axis participates in atlanto-axial joints with the atlas.
rationales.d: Occipital condyles articulate with the superior articular facets of the atlas.

marrow__ANAT_CH59_Q006.takeaway: Rotation of the head occurs primarily at the median atlanto-axial pivot joint around the dens.
marrow__ANAT_CH59_Q006.displayText:
Rotation of the head occurs primarily at the median atlanto-axial pivot joint around the dens.

Movements at the atlanto-axial joint allow a person to look left and right.

The atlanto-axial joints include a median pivot joint between the dens and the ring formed by the anterior arch and transverse atlantal ligament, plus paired lateral synovial joints. Movement is almost exclusively rotation around the axis; normal range is about 40 degrees.
emphasis: Rotation of the head occurs primarily at the median atlanto-axial pivot joint around the dens

rationales.a: Atlanto-occipital joints mainly permit flexion and extension, the nodding movement.
rationales.c: C2–C3 allows cervical movement but is not the primary pivot for side-to-side head rotation.
rationales.d: C3–C4 is a lower cervical joint and does not provide the main axial rotation mechanism.

marrow__ANAT_CH59_Q007.takeaway: The transverse atlantal ligament is the horizontal component of the cruciform ligament stabilizing the dens against the atlas.
marrow__ANAT_CH59_Q007.displayText:
The transverse atlantal ligament is the horizontal component of the cruciform ligament stabilizing the dens against the atlas.

The transverse atlantal ligament is a component of the cruciform ligament at the atlanto-axial joints.

Cruciform ligaments are cross-shaped. The horizontal component is the transverse atlantal ligament, attached on each side to lateral masses of atlas and retaining the dens. The vertical component is formed by superior and inferior longitudinal ligaments.
emphasis: The transverse atlantal ligament is the horizontal component of the cruciform ligament stabilizing the dens against the atlas

rationales.b: Ligamenta flava link adjacent vertebral laminae; they do not include the transverse atlantal ligament.
rationales.c: The anterior longitudinal ligament runs along vertebral bodies and is separate from the atlas stabilizer.
rationales.d: The posterior longitudinal ligament lies on vertebral bodies within the canal and is not the cruciform complex.

marrow__ANAT_CH59_Q008.takeaway: Whiplash hyperextension can strain the anterior longitudinal ligament along the anterior vertebral bodies.
marrow__ANAT_CH59_Q008.displayText:
Whiplash hyperextension can strain the anterior longitudinal ligament along the anterior vertebral bodies.

The clinical scenario is suggestive of whiplash injury, in which the anterior longitudinal ligament of the spine is damaged.

Whiplash is a cervical acceleration-deceleration injury with hyperextension followed by recoil flexion. The anterior longitudinal ligament is a strong band along the anterior vertebral bodies, extending from the basilar occiput to upper sacrum and attaching at the anterior tubercle of C1 and body of C2.
emphasis: Whiplash hyperextension can strain the anterior longitudinal ligament along the anterior vertebral bodies

rationales.a: Interspinous ligament lies between spinous processes posteriorly and is not the ligament classically strained by hyperextension.
rationales.b: Posterior longitudinal ligament is behind vertebral bodies within the canal; hyperflexion is more likely to tension posterior restraints.
rationales.c: Supraspinous ligament connects spinous-process tips and is not the principal anterior restraint in hyperextension.

marrow__ANAT_CH59_Q009.takeaway: The tectorial membrane is the cranial continuation of the posterior longitudinal ligament over the dens and upper cervical joints.
marrow__ANAT_CH59_Q009.displayText:
The tectorial membrane is the cranial continuation of the posterior longitudinal ligament over the dens and upper cervical joints.

Membrana tectoria (tectorial membrane) is the cranial continuation of the posterior longitudinal ligament.

The posterior longitudinal ligament lies in the vertebral canal on the posterior surfaces of vertebral bodies, extends from the axis to the sacrum, and above the axis continues as membrana tectoria to the foramen magnum.
emphasis: The tectorial membrane is the cranial continuation of the posterior longitudinal ligament over the dens and upper cervical joints

rationales.a: The anterior atlanto-occipital membrane is an anterior membrane, not the continuation forming the tectorial membrane.
rationales.b: The posterior atlanto-occipital membrane covers the posterior foramen magnum/atlas interval, not the tectorial continuation.
rationales.c: Anterior longitudinal ligament continues cranially as the anterior atlanto-occipital membrane, not tectorial membrane.

marrow__ANAT_CH59_Q010.takeaway: Lumbar facet orientation restricts axial rotation; lumbar movement is dominated by flexion and extension.
marrow__ANAT_CH59_Q010.displayText:
Lumbar facet orientation restricts axial rotation; lumbar movement is dominated by flexion and extension.

Rotation is anatomically restricted in the lumbar region. The source clinical vignette is suggestive of carcinoma prostate metastatic to the lumbar spine.

Flexion is accompanied by relaxation of the anterior longitudinal ligament and compression of the anterior intervertebral discs; flexion is most effective in the thoracic region. Extension is greater in cervical and lumbar regions, lateral flexion is accompanied by axial rotation, and axial rotation is greatest in the cervical region at the atlanto-axial joint. Lumbar regions have very little rotation.
emphasis: Lumbar facet orientation restricts axial rotation; lumbar movement is dominated by flexion and extension

rationales.a: The lumbar spine permits substantial flexion; it is not the most restricted movement.
rationales.b: Extension is also an important lumbar movement and is not the one most restricted by facet orientation.
rationales.c: Lateral flexion occurs in the lumbar spine more than rotation.

marrow__ANAT_CH59_Q011.takeaway: The hemiazygos vein typically crosses to the right around T8, not T5.
marrow__ANAT_CH59_Q011.displayText:
The hemiazygos vein typically crosses to the right around T8, not T5.

The scenario is suggestive of Brown-Sequard syndrome due to vertebral-column injury. The false landmark is that the hemiazygos vein crosses from left to right at T5; the source states it crosses at T8 (and not T5).
emphasis: The hemiazygos vein typically crosses to the right around T8, not T5

rationales.a: The heart spans approximately T5–T8 in the recumbent source landmark description.
rationales.b: The superior vena cava enters the right atrium near the T5 level.
rationales.c: The azygos vein arches to join the SVC around T5.

marrow__ANAT_CH59_Q012.takeaway: A lumbar puncture passes through posterior ligaments and ligamentum flavum but does not pierce the posterior longitudinal ligament, which is anterior to the canal.
marrow__ANAT_CH59_Q012.displayText:
A lumbar puncture passes through posterior ligaments and ligamentum flavum but does not pierce the posterior longitudinal ligament, which is anterior to the canal.

A lumbar puncture is planned for suspected Guillain-Barré syndrome. The posterior longitudinal ligament is not pierced during lumbar puncture.

Structures pierced during lumbar puncture, in order, are skin, subcutaneous tissue, supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament, ligamentum flavum, epidural space, dura mater and arachnoid mater.
emphasis: A lumbar puncture passes through posterior ligaments and ligamentum flavum but does not pierce the posterior longitudinal ligament, which is anterior to the canal

rationales.a: The needle traverses ligamentum flavum before entering the epidural space.
rationales.b: The interspinous ligament lies in the midline path between adjacent spinous processes.
rationales.d: The supraspinous ligament is also crossed in a midline approach before the deeper ligaments.

marrow__ANAT_CH59_Q013.takeaway: The triangle of auscultation is bounded by trapezius, latissimus dorsi and the medial border of the scapula; serratus anterior is not a boundary.
marrow__ANAT_CH59_Q013.displayText:
The triangle of auscultation is bounded by trapezius, latissimus dorsi and the medial border of the scapula; serratus anterior is not a boundary.

Serratus anterior is not a boundary of the triangle of auscultation. This region has fewer impedances between the stethoscope and lungs and permits better auscultation of the patient.

Boundaries: medially trapezius lateral border; laterally scapula medial border; inferiorly latissimus dorsi upper border. The floor includes the 5th and 7th ribs, 6th intercostal space and rhomboid major.
emphasis: The triangle of auscultation is bounded by trapezius, latissimus dorsi and the medial border of the scapula; serratus anterior is not a boundary

rationales.a: The medial border of the scapula forms one boundary of the auscultation triangle.
rationales.c: Latissimus dorsi forms the inferolateral boundary.

marrow__ANAT_CH59_Q014.takeaway: The image marks levator scapulae, which receives motor supply from the dorsal scapular nerve (with cervical contributions).
marrow__ANAT_CH59_Q014.displayText:
The image marks levator scapulae, which receives motor supply from the dorsal scapular nerve (with cervical contributions).

The muscle marked by the arrow is levator scapulae, which is innervated by the dorsal scapular nerve.

The source table lists selected appendicular muscles of the back and their nerve supply: trapezius-accessory nerve, latissimus dorsi-thoracodorsal nerve, levator scapulae-dorsal scapular nerve, rhomboid major/minor-dorsal scapular nerve. It also notes the suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus, while subscapular nerves supply teres major and subscapularis.
emphasis: The image marks levator scapulae, which receives motor supply from the dorsal scapular nerve (with cervical contributions)

rationales.b: The suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus, not levator scapulae.
rationales.c: Dorsal rami of C1 do not supply levator scapulae; dorsal scapular nerve is the named motor supply.
rationales.d: Subscapular nerves supply subscapularis and teres major, not levator scapulae.
